Matter.q: Which of these is NOT matter?
wrong: The air inside a balloon, even though you can't see it
Air has mass and takes up space, so it is matter.
A drop of water on a leaf
Sand has mass and takes up space.
Matter.exp: Matter must have mass and take up space; light does neither.

Matter.q: A student says air isn't matter because you can't see it. What is the best reply?
Matter.right: Air has mass and takes up space
wrong: He is right, because matter must be something you can see or touch
Being visible is not part of the definition.
Air is matter only when it is cold
Temperature doesn't decide whether something is matter.
Air is matter only inside a container
Air has mass and volume anywhere.
Matter.exp: Anything with mass that takes up space is matter, visible or not.

Solid.q: You move an iron bar from a small box to a large box. What happens to its shape and volume?
wrong: Its shape changes to fit the bigger box but its volume stays the same
Both change to fill the box
Its volume grows but its shape stays
Solid.exp: A solid has a fixed shape and a fixed volume.

Solid.q: Why does a diamond keep its shape no matter what container it is in?
Solid.right: Its particles are locked in rigid positions
wrong: Its particles are far apart and move randomly around the container
Its particles have stopped moving completely
Its particles slide past each other
Solid.exp: Solid particles are close together and locked in place, though they still vibrate.

Liquid.q: You pour 200 mL of water from a tall glass into a wide bowl. What happens?
Liquid.right: The shape changes; the volume stays 200 mL
wrong: The shape stays the same and the volume spreads out to fill the bowl
A liquid takes its container's shape, and its volume is fixed.
Both the shape and the volume change
A liquid takes the shape of its container.
Liquid.exp: A liquid has a definite volume but takes the shape of its container.

Liquid.q: Blood flows through your blood vessels and fills whatever shape they have. Which particle picture explains this?
Liquid.right: Close together but able to move around
wrong: Far apart and moving randomly, hitting the walls of the vessels
That is a gas; blood is a liquid.
Liquid.exp: Liquid particles are close together but can move, so a liquid flows and takes its container's shape.

Gas.q: A small amount of helium is released into an empty room. What happens to it?
Gas.right: It spreads to fill the whole room
wrong: It stays in one small cloud near the tank, keeping its own volume
A gas has no fixed volume.
It sinks to the floor and forms a puddle
It keeps the shape of the tank
A gas has no fixed shape.
Gas.exp: A gas takes both the shape and the volume of its container.

Gas.q: Why can you squeeze a lot more air into a bike tire, but not more water into a full bottle?
wrong: Water particles are far apart and air particles are packed tightly
Air is matter, so it has mass.
Water in a bottle is a liquid.
Gas.exp: Gas particles are far apart with lots of empty space between them, so a gas has no fixed volume.

Ice (solid water).q: An ice cube keeps its cube shape on a plate. What are its water molecules doing?
wrong: Moving far apart and hitting the plate and the air around it
Breaking apart into hydrogen and oxygen
Ice (solid water).exp: In ice the molecules are locked in rigid positions, close together.

Ice (solid water).q: Compare the spacing of the molecules in ice and in steam.
Ice (solid water).right: Close together in ice, far apart in steam
wrong: Far apart in ice and close together in steam, because steam is hotter
There are no molecules in steam
Ice (solid water).exp: Ice molecules are close and locked in place; steam molecules are far apart.

Liquid water.q: How does liquid water differ from ice at the particle level?
wrong: Its molecules are far apart and hit the walls of the container
Its molecules are different from ice's
Its molecules are locked in place
Liquid water.exp: Liquid water molecules are still close together, but they can move around to some extent.

Liquid water.q: Water poured on a table spreads out but stays as one puddle instead of filling the room. Why?
Liquid water.right: Its molecules are close but can move
wrong: Its molecules are far apart and move randomly in every direction
Its molecules are locked in rigid positions
Liquid water.exp: Close-together molecules that can still slide around give a liquid its definite volume and changing shape.

Steam (gaseous water).q: Steam in a closed pot pushes on the lid. What are the water molecules doing?
Steam (gaseous water).right: Moving randomly and hitting the walls
wrong: Holding fixed positions close together against the lid
Sliding past each other at the bottom of the pot
Splitting into hydrogen and oxygen gas
Steam (gaseous water).exp: Steam molecules are far apart, moving randomly and hitting each other and the container walls.

Steam (gaseous water).q: Which state of water has its molecules farthest apart?
wrong: Ice, because it is the coldest of the three states of water
Spacing changes from state to state.
Steam (gaseous water).exp: In steam the molecules are far apart and moving randomly.

Intact molecules.q: Ice melts into water and the water boils into steam. What happens to the H₂O molecules?
Intact molecules.right: They stay H₂O; only motion and spacing change
wrong: They break into hydrogen and oxygen atoms when the water turns to steam
The molecules stay intact; boiling is physical.
They turn into a new substance
Only the spacing changes, not the molecules.
Intact molecules.exp: In ice, liquid water and steam the H₂O molecules are intact; only their motion and distance apart change.

Intact molecules.q: Why is boiling water a physical change and not a chemical one?
wrong: Bubbles form, and bubbles always mean that a new substance was made
These bubbles are still water vapor.
Adding heat doesn't decide the type of change.
A temperature rise alone doesn't decide it.
Intact molecules.exp: The molecules don't change; only their motion and spacing do, so no new substance forms.

Solid particles.q: A drawing shows particles in neat rows, touching, each with short wiggle lines. Which state is it?
wrong: Gas, because the particles are moving, as the wiggle lines show
Gas particles are far apart and not in rows.
Liquid particles aren't in orderly rows.
Solid particles.exp: Closely packed, orderly particles that vibrate in place are a solid.

Solid particles.q: Do the particles in a solid move at all?
Solid particles.right: Yes, they vibrate in fixed positions
wrong: No, they are perfectly still until the solid melts into a liquid
Yes, they slide past each other
Yes, they move fast and randomly
Solid particles.exp: Solid particles vibrate in place; they are closely packed and orderly.

Liquid particles.q: Which drawing best shows a liquid?
Liquid particles.right: Particles touching but in no fixed pattern
wrong: Particles far apart with long arrows pointing in random directions
A liquid is made of many particles.
Liquid particles.exp: Liquid particles are close together but slide past each other, so they have no fixed pattern.

Liquid particles.q: Why can you stir a liquid with a spoon but not a solid?
Liquid particles.right: Liquid particles slide past each other
wrong: Liquid particles are far apart with empty space between them for the spoon
Liquid particles.exp: In a liquid the particles are close together but can slide past each other.

Gas particles.q: Why can you smell perfume across a room a short time after it is sprayed?
Gas particles.right: Gas particles move fast and randomly
wrong: The perfume particles are locked in place and the smell travels as heat
Gas particles are not locked in place.
The particles slide slowly along the floor
That's not how a gas behaves.
Sprayed perfume becomes a gas in the air.
Gas particles.exp: Gas particles are far apart and move fast and randomly, so they spread through the room.

Gas particles.q: Of the three states, which has the least order in its particles?
wrong: Solid, because its particles are always vibrating back and forth
Solid particles are the most orderly.
Liquid particles are still close together.
Order drops from solid to gas.
Gas particles.exp: Gas particles are far apart and move randomly, the least ordered state.

Energy and state.q: Put the three states of the same substance in order from least to most energy.
wrong: Gas, liquid, solid, since gas particles are the farthest apart
Energy and state.exp: Energy increases from solid to liquid to gas.

Energy and state.q: You add heat to a substance and it changes state. What happens to its particles?
wrong: Less motion and more order, since heat makes them settle into place
They turn into a new substance
A change of state is physical.
Energy and state.exp: More energy means more motion and less order.

Melting.q: Butter left in a hot pan turns from a solid into a liquid. What happens to its particles?
Melting.right: They speed up and become less organized
wrong: They slow down and settle into a more organized pattern than before
They break apart into new substances
Particles speed up when something melts.
Melting.exp: Melting is solid to liquid: the particles speed up and become less organized.

Melting.q: A chocolate bar melts in your pocket. What kind of change is it?
wrong: Chemical, because it changed from a solid into a liquid
A change of state is physical.
Warming alone doesn't make a change chemical.
Melting.exp: Melting is a physical change: the substance stays the same.

Melting.q: Which of these is the same kind of change as melting ice?
Melting.right: Melting a candle on a hot plate
wrong: Burning a candle until the wax is used up and only smoke is left
Melting.exp: Melting is always a physical change of state.

Melting.q: Ice is melted and the water is refrozen. What does this show about melting?
Melting.right: It is physical; the water is still water
wrong: It is chemical, because the ice can't come back after the water is frozen
It comes back; melting is physical.
Melting.exp: Melting is a physical change of state.

Freezing.q: Water in an ice tray turns to ice in the freezer. Which change is this, and what do the particles do?
wrong: Melting; the particles speed up and become less organized as they cool
Deposition is gas to solid, and particles slow down.
Freezing.exp: Freezing is liquid to solid: the particles slow down and become more organized.

Freezing.q: Melted candle wax hardens again as it cools. Is it a new substance?
Freezing.right: No, freezing is a physical change
wrong: Yes, because hardening always means a chemical reaction has happened
Liquid to solid is freezing, a physical change.
A change in shape is physical.
Cooling alone doesn't make a new substance.
Freezing.exp: Freezing (liquid to solid) is a physical change.

Evaporation or boiling.q: A puddle disappears on a sunny day. Which change of state happened?
wrong: Condensation, because the water moved from the ground into the air
The water is still water, now as a vapor.
Evaporation or boiling.exp: Evaporation is liquid to gas, a physical change.

Evaporation or boiling.q: When water boils, how do its particles change?
Evaporation or boiling.right: They speed up and become less organized
wrong: They slow down and become more organized as they leave the pot
They split into hydrogen and oxygen
They speed up and spread out.
Evaporation or boiling.exp: Boiling is liquid to gas: the particles speed up and become less organized.

Condensation.q: Drops of water form on the outside of a cold glass of lemonade. Which change of state is this?
wrong: Evaporation of lemonade leaking out through tiny holes in the glass
The water comes from the air, gas to liquid.
Condensation.exp: Water vapor in the air turns to liquid on the cold glass: gas to liquid is condensation.

Condensation.q: When steam hits a cold mirror and turns to liquid, what do the water particles do?
Condensation.right: Slow down and become more organized
wrong: Speed up and become less organized as they touch the cold mirror
Condensation.exp: Condensation is gas to liquid: the particles slow down and become more organized.

Sublimation.q: Dry ice (solid carbon dioxide) turns directly into gas without melting. Which change is this?
wrong: Evaporation, since a gas forms from the substance as it warms up
Sublimation.exp: Solid straight to gas, skipping the liquid, is sublimation.

Sublimation.q: Which pair of changes both make the particles speed up and become less organized?
wrong: Deposition and freezing, since both of them start from a gas or a liquid
Both of those slow particles down.
Sublimation.exp: Sublimation (solid to gas) and melting (solid to liquid) both speed particles up.

Deposition.q: On a cold night, water vapor in the air forms frost directly on a car window. Which change is this?
wrong: Freezing, because the window is cold enough to turn the water into ice
Freezing starts from a liquid; this starts from a gas.
Deposition.exp: Gas straight to solid, skipping the liquid, is deposition.

Deposition.q: Deposition is the reverse of which change?
wrong: Condensation, because both of them start with a gas and end with less motion
Deposition.exp: Deposition is gas to solid; sublimation is solid to gas.

Speed up or slow down.q: In which group do ALL the changes make the particles slow down?
wrong: Melting, boiling and sublimation, which all need heat to be added
Melting and boiling speed particles up.
Speed up or slow down.exp: Freezing, condensation and deposition move to more organized states, so particles slow down.

Speed up or slow down.q: A substance's particles slow down and become more organized. What can you conclude?
Speed up or slow down.right: It moved to a more ordered state
wrong: A chemical reaction happened and the substance became something new
All six changes of state are physical.
It moved to a less ordered state
Speed up or slow down.exp: Slowing down means moving to a state with more organization, such as freezing, condensation or deposition.

Water at 0 °C.q: A glass of ice water sits at exactly 0 °C. Which states of water are present?
wrong: Only solid, because 0 °C is the temperature at which all water must freeze
At 0 °C ice and liquid water exist together.
Some molecules escape as vapor too.
Water at 0 °C.exp: At 0 °C ice and liquid water sit in equilibrium, and some molecules escape as vapor.

Water at 0 °C.q: At 0 °C, how can water vapor be present even though water boils at 100 °C?
Water at 0 °C.right: Some molecules escape from the surface
wrong: The ice is boiling, because 0 °C is the boiling point of solid water
Water vapor can only exist at 100 °C
Vapor forms by evaporation and sublimation below boiling.
The vapor is a new substance
Water at 0 °C.exp: Some molecules escape into the air by evaporation from the liquid and sublimation from the ice.

Absolute zero (0 K).q: Why are there no negative numbers on the Kelvin scale?
Absolute zero (0 K).right: It starts at the coldest possible temperature
wrong: Kelvin only measures temperatures above the freezing point of water
Kelvin starts much lower, at absolute zero.
Negative numbers are rounded to zero
Nothing can be colder than 0 K.
Absolute zero (0 K).exp: The Kelvin scale starts at absolute zero, the lowest possible temperature.

Absolute zero (0 K).q: A sample is cooled to 0 K. What is true of its particles?
Absolute zero (0 K).right: They have their minimum possible motion
wrong: They move faster than ever, because energy builds up when it is cold
Absolute zero (0 K).exp: At absolute zero (−273.15 °C) particles have their minimum possible motion.

Physical property.q: Which of these is a physical property of copper?
wrong: It turns green when it reacts with the air over many years
Reacting into something new is a chemical property.
Physical property.exp: Color can be observed without changing the copper into something else.

Physical property.q: You measure a metal's density. Afterwards, is it still the same metal?
Physical property.right: Yes; density is a physical property
wrong: No, because measuring a property always changes the substance a little bit
Physical properties are measured without changing the substance.
No; density is a chemical property
Only if it is a liquid
Physical property.exp: A physical property can be observed or measured without changing the substance.

Chemical property.q: Which statement describes a chemical property of wood?
wrong: It floats in water because it is less dense than the water around it
Chemical property.exp: Being able to change into new substances (burning) is a chemical property.

Chemical property.q: To find out a substance's chemical property, what usually has to happen?
Chemical property.right: It has to change into a new substance
wrong: You only need to look at it closely under a bright light or a microscope
Chemical property.exp: A chemical property is the ability to change into a new substance, so you see it when that happens.

Intensive property.q: You cut a gold bar in half. Which property is the same for each half as for the whole bar?
wrong: Mass, because both halves are made of exactly the same kind of gold
Mass halves; it depends on amount.
Intensive property.exp: Density doesn't depend on how much you have, so it's intensive.

Intensive property.q: A teaspoon and a pot of the same water both boil at the same temperature. What does this show about boiling point?
Intensive property.right: It doesn't depend on the amount
wrong: It depends on how much water there is, so a bigger pot boils hotter
The two boil at the same temperature.
Intensive property.exp: Boiling point is an intensive property: it doesn't depend on amount.

Extensive property.q: Which of these would double if you doubled the amount of a substance?
wrong: Density, because there is twice as much matter packed into the sample
Boiling point doesn't change with amount.
Extensive property.exp: Volume depends on the amount of substance, so it's extensive.

Extensive property.q: Why can't you identify a substance by its mass alone?
Extensive property.right: Mass changes with how much you have
wrong: Mass is a chemical property, so you would have to destroy the sample first
All substances have the same mass
Extensive property.exp: Mass is extensive, so any substance can have any mass. Intensive properties like density help identify a substance.

Physical properties you observe.q: Which physical property can you find with your senses alone, without an instrument?
wrong: Boiling point, which you can feel when the liquid gets hot enough
Physical properties you observe.exp: Odor, color and state are observed; density and melting and boiling points are measured.

Physical properties you observe.q: A student notes that a sample is a yellow solid. What kind of properties did the student record?
wrong: Chemical properties, because the student is describing what the sample is like
Color and state don't involve a new substance.
Color and state need no instrument.
Color and state don't depend on amount.
Physical properties you observe.exp: Color and state are physical properties you observe.

Physical properties you measure.q: Which physical property needs an instrument to find?
wrong: Color, which you have to see under the proper light to be sure of
Physical properties you measure.exp: Volume, density, melting point, boiling point and hardness are measured.

Physical properties you measure.q: A student uses a graduated cylinder on a liquid. Which physical property is she most likely finding?
wrong: Flammability, by checking how quickly the liquid burns in the cylinder
Physical properties you measure.exp: A graduated cylinder measures volume, a measured physical property.

Ethyl alcohol boiling at 78°C is an exam.q: Water boils at 100 °C and ethyl alcohol at 78 °C. What do both boiling points describe?
Ethyl alcohol boiling at 78°C is an exam.right: A physical property of each liquid
wrong: A chemical property, because each liquid turns into something different
No new substance forms when a liquid boils.
Boiling point doesn't depend on amount.
Ethyl alcohol boiling at 78°C is an exam.exp: Boiling point is a physical property; the boiling itself is a physical change.

Ethyl alcohol boiling at 78°C is an exam.q: Alcohol vapor from boiling is cooled and turns back into liquid alcohol. What does this show about the boiling?
wrong: A new substance formed and then reacted back into alcohol when it cooled
Boiling is only a change of state.
Ethyl alcohol boiling at 78°C is an exam.exp: Boiling is a change of state, a physical change; the vapor is still alcohol.

Sugar fermenting to form ethyl alcohol i.q: Yeast turns the sugar in grape juice into alcohol. Why is this a chemical change?
wrong: The juice changes from a solid into a liquid as the sugar disappears
The juice is a liquid the whole time.
Warming alone doesn't make a change chemical.
Dissolving doesn't make a new substance.
Sugar fermenting to form ethyl alcohol i.exp: Fermenting makes alcohol, a new substance, so it's chemical.

Sugar fermenting to form ethyl alcohol i.q: Which pair correctly classifies the two changes?
Sugar fermenting to form ethyl alcohol i.right: Alcohol boiling: physical; sugar fermenting: chemical
wrong: Alcohol boiling: chemical; sugar fermenting: physical, since no flame is involved
Boiling doesn't make a new substance.
Sugar fermenting to form ethyl alcohol i.exp: Boiling is a change of state; fermenting forms a new substance.

Flammability.q: Gasoline catches fire easily but water does not. What property is being compared?
wrong: Boiling point, a physical property of the two liquids being compared
Catching fire is about burning, not boiling.
Burning makes new substances, so it's chemical.
Flammability.exp: Flammability is the ability to burn, a chemical property.

Flammability.q: Why is flammability a chemical property and not a physical one?
wrong: You can see a flame with your eyes, so it is observed without any instrument
Being visible doesn't make it physical.
Physical properties can also be measured.
Flammability.exp: Flammability is chemical because burning turns a substance into new substances.

Rusting of steel.q: A steel bike left in the rain develops a flaky reddish coating. What happened?
Rusting of steel.right: The steel reacted with oxygen to form rust
wrong: The steel melted a little in the rain and then hardened again as a coating
Rust is a new substance, not melted steel.
Rust comes from the steel itself.
Rusting of steel.exp: Steel reacting with oxygen to form rust is a chemical property in action.

Rusting of steel.q: Is steel's ability to rust a physical or chemical property?
Rusting of steel.right: Chemical: rust is a new substance
wrong: Physical, because you can see the color change from silver to reddish-brown
Seeing it doesn't make it physical; rust is new.
Rusting of steel.exp: Rusting forms a new substance, so it's a chemical property.

Digestion of food.q: Bread is chewed into smaller pieces and then broken down into new substances in your body. Which step is chemical?
Digestion of food.right: Breaking it down into new substances
wrong: Chewing it into small pieces, since the bread becomes smaller and softer
Chewing only changes size, a physical change.
Chewing alone doesn't make new substances.
Digestion of food.exp: Digestion breaks food into new substances, a chemical process.

Digestion of food.q: Why is digestion listed as a chemical property of food?
wrong: Food changes shape and size as it moves through your stomach and intestines
Food gets warm in your body
Digestion of food.exp: Food is broken down into new substances, so digestion shows a chemical property.

Reacting with acid.q: Vinegar is poured on chalk and it bubbles. What does this show about chalk?
Reacting with acid.right: It reacts with acid, a chemical property
wrong: It dissolves in vinegar, which is a physical property of the chalk
The bubbles show a reaction, not just dissolving.
It has a low boiling point
Bubbles here come from a reaction, not boiling.
Reacting with acid.exp: Reacting with an acid such as vinegar is a chemical property.

Reacting with acid.q: Which property tells you something about how a substance reacts, rather than how it looks?
wrong: Its color, which can change depending on what kind of light hits it
Reacting with acid.exp: Reacting with an acid is a chemical property.

Other chemical properties.q: Which item from the review sheet's list is a chemical property?
wrong: Being shiny, like a metal that reflects light well
Other chemical properties.exp: The review sheet lists corrosive, toxic, pH and reacting with oxygen or water as chemical properties.

Other chemical properties.q: A label says a cleaner is corrosive. What kind of property is that?
wrong: A physical property, because you can read it on the bottle without opening it
Where you read it doesn't matter; corrosive is chemical.
It isn't a change of state.
Other chemical properties.exp: Being corrosive is on the review sheet's list of chemical properties.

Physical change.q: Which of these is a physical change?
wrong: Burning a piece of paper until only ash and smoke are left behind
Physical change.exp: Crushing changes shape only; the metal's composition stays the same.

Physical change.q: Water freezes into ice. What happens to its chemical bonds?
wrong: They break apart and then form again in a new way as the water cools
A physical change doesn't break bonds.
New bonds form a new substance
Physical change.exp: In a physical change, composition stays the same and bonds aren't broken.

Chemical change.q: Which of these is a chemical change?
wrong: Melting butter in a pan so that it can be mixed into the batter
Chemical change.exp: Baking turns the ingredients into new substances.

Chemical change.q: In a chemical change, what happens to the atoms?
Chemical change.right: They are reorganized into new substances
wrong: They stay arranged the same way but move farther apart from each other
That describes a change of state.
Chemical change.exp: In a chemical change the atoms are reorganized into new substances with different properties.

Reaction.q: A Bunsen burner burns methane with oxygen to make carbon dioxide and water. What is this?
wrong: A physical change, because the methane only changes from one state to another
Reaction.exp: A reaction is a chemical change; methane and oxygen become new substances.

Reaction.q: A teacher says, "This reaction makes a gas." What kind of change is she describing?
wrong: A physical change, because gases are always made by heating something up
Reaction.exp: Reaction is another name for a chemical change.

Precipitate.q: Two clear liquids are mixed and a cloudy solid appears. What does this solid suggest?
wrong: One of the liquids froze when the two of them were poured together
A precipitate comes from a reaction.
A new solid is a sign of change.
Precipitate.exp: A precipitate is a new solid, a sign of a chemical change.

Precipitate.right: A solid forming when two liquids mix
wrong: Ice forming when liquid water is put in a freezer overnight
Precipitate.exp: A precipitate is a solid that forms when substances react.

Gas given off.q: Baking soda and vinegar fizz when mixed. What does the fizzing show?
wrong: The vinegar is boiling because the baking soda heated it up quickly
The bubbles are a new gas, not boiling.
Air was trapped in the powder
The gas is made by a reaction.
Bubbles from mixing are a sign of a reaction.
Gas given off.exp: Bubbles of a new gas are a sign of a chemical change.

Gas given off.q: A student smells something sharp in a beaker and says a chemical change happened. What is wrong with this reasoning?
wrong: Nothing is wrong, since any smell always comes from a chemical reaction
Odor alone still isn't a sign.
A smell just isn't enough evidence.
Gas given off.exp: Odor is a physical property, so a smell alone isn't a sign of a chemical change.

Color change.q: A cut apple turns brown in the air. Which sign suggests a chemical change?
wrong: The smaller size of the apple pieces after it has been cut up
Staying solid isn't a sign of change.
Color change.exp: A new color can show that a new substance was made.

Color change.q: Why is a color change only a possible sign of a chemical change, not proof?
Color change.right: Color can change without a new substance
wrong: A color change always means a new substance was made in a reaction
A color change alone isn't proof.
Color change.exp: A new color can show a new substance, but it is a clue, not proof (adding food coloring changes color too).

Temperature change.q: Two solutions are mixed and the beaker gets hot on its own. What does this suggest?
wrong: A physical change, because heating something only changes how fast it moves
Getting hot on its own is a sign of a reaction.
A beaker doesn't warm up by itself.
Temperature change.exp: A mixture getting hotter or colder on its own is a sign of a chemical change.

Temperature change.q: Two liquids are mixed in a test tube, and the tube turns cold by itself without being cooled. Which sign is this?
wrong: A precipitate, since a solid must form whenever two liquids are mixed
Temperature change.exp: Getting colder on its own is a temperature change, a sign of a reaction.

Light given off.q: A glow stick glows after you bend it. Which sign of a chemical change is this?
wrong: A precipitate, because something inside the stick turns into a solid
It's a glow, light given off.
Light given off.exp: A glow shows a reaction giving off energy as light.

Light given off.q: A light bulb glows when switched on. Why isn't that a sign of a chemical change?
wrong: It is a chemical change, because any light means a reaction is happening
Light alone isn't proof; the bulb doesn't change.
Light bulbs don't give off light
Light given off.exp: A flame or glow from a reaction is a sign, but a bulb glowing makes no new substance.

Boiling.q: A student says boiling water is chemical because bubbles form. What is the best correction?
wrong: The student is right, because bubbles always mean that a new gas was made
Boiling.exp: Boiling is a physical change: the bubbles are water as a gas.

Boiling.q: Which pair contains one physical change and one chemical change?
wrong: Boiling water; melting ice, since both of them require heat to happen
Boiling.exp: Boiling is physical; electrolysis splits water into new substances.

Electrolysis of water (decomposition).q: An electric current is passed through water and two gases bubble out. What are they?
wrong: Water vapor from both ends, since the current heats the water until it boils
Electrolysis of water (decomposition).exp: Electrolysis splits water (H₂O) into hydrogen (H₂) and oxygen (O₂).

Electrolysis of water (decomposition).q: In electrolysis, 2 H₂O make 2 H₂ and 1 O₂. Why is this a decomposition?
wrong: Two substances combine to form one new and different substance
One element pushes another out of a compound
Electrolysis of water (decomposition).exp: Decomposition breaks one substance into two or more; water becomes hydrogen and oxygen.

Combustion (burning).q: Wood burns in a fireplace and leaves ash. Which change happened?
Combustion (burning).right: A chemical change: new substances formed
wrong: A physical change, because the wood only changed from a solid to a gas and ash
Ash and gases are new substances.
Combustion (burning).exp: Combustion reacts a substance with oxygen, giving off heat and light and forming new substances.

Combustion (burning).q: What does every combustion need, according to your card?
wrong: Water, because burning can't happen unless the fuel is wet enough first
Combustion (burning).exp: In combustion a substance reacts with oxygen.

Rusting.q: An iron gate rusts. Which substances combined?
wrong: Iron and hydrogen, which come from the water that falls on the gate as rain
Rust forms from iron and oxygen.
Rusting.exp: Iron combines with oxygen to form rust (iron oxide).

Rusting.q: Rusting is iron + oxygen making one new substance. Which type of reaction is that?
wrong: Decomposition, because the iron breaks down and falls apart into flakes
Rusting.exp: Two substances combining to form something new is synthesis.

Synthesis.q: Hydrogen and oxygen combine to form water. Which type of reaction is this?
wrong: Decomposition, because the hydrogen and oxygen are broken into water
Decomposition breaks one substance into two or more.
Synthesis.exp: Two or more substances combining to form something new is synthesis.

Synthesis.q: Synthesis is the reverse of which reaction type?
wrong: Double displacement, since both of them involve two substances at the start
Synthesis builds up; decomposition breaks down.
That's an element pushing another out.
Synthesis.exp: Synthesis builds something up; decomposition breaks something down.

Decomposition.q: Heating a compound breaks it into a metal and a gas. Which type of reaction is this?
wrong: Synthesis, because two products were made from the substance by heating it
Decomposition.exp: One substance breaking into two or more is decomposition.

Decomposition.q: Which example from your cards is a decomposition?
wrong: Rusting of iron, because the iron slowly falls apart into flakes of rust
Decomposition.exp: Electrolysis breaks water into hydrogen and oxygen.

Single displacement.q: Zinc is placed in a copper compound and pushes the copper out, taking its place. Which type of reaction is this?
wrong: Double displacement, since zinc and copper both end up in a different place
Only one element pushes another out of one compound.
Single displacement.exp: One element pushing another out of a compound is single displacement.

Single displacement.q: How does single displacement differ from double displacement?
wrong: Two compounds trade their positive elements with each other at the same time
Single displacement.exp: Single: one element is pushed out of a compound. Double: the positive elements of two compounds switch.

Double displacement.q: AB + CD → AD + CB. Which type of reaction is this?
wrong: Single displacement, because one element pushes another out of the compound
Double displacement.exp: The positive elements switch places between the two compounds.

Double displacement.q: Two salt solutions are mixed, the partners swap, and a precipitate forms. Which reaction type best fits?
wrong: Decomposition, because the solid falls out of the solution as it breaks apart
Double displacement.exp: When the positive elements of two compounds switch places, it's double displacement.

Element.q: A sample can't be broken into anything simpler, even by electrolysis or heating. What is it?
wrong: A compound, since compounds always stay together no matter what you do
Compounds can be broken down chemically.
Element.exp: An element can't be broken down into other substances by chemical methods.

Element.q: Which of these is an element?
wrong: H₂O, because it is made of hydrogen and oxygen joined together
Two types of atoms make it a compound.
Two types of atoms: a compound.
Element.exp: O₂ has only one type of atom (one capital letter), so it is an element.

Compound.q: Electrolysis breaks a pure liquid into two different gases. What was the liquid?
wrong: An element, because it was pure and had only one substance in it at the start
Elements can't be broken down chemically.
Compound.exp: A compound can be broken into its elements by chemical methods.

Compound.q: Why is water always H₂O, whether it comes from a lake or a lab?
Compound.right: A compound always has the same composition
wrong: Water is a mixture, and all mixtures keep the same recipe wherever they are
It has two types of atoms.
Compound.exp: A compound has a fixed combination of elements.

Pure substance.q: Which list contains only pure substances?
wrong: Air, salt water and gold, since each of them looks the same throughout
Air and salt water are mixtures.
Pure substance.exp: A pure substance is an element or a compound: it always has the same composition.

Pure substance.q: A sample always has exactly the same makeup, but electrolysis can split it. What is it?
Pure substance.right: A compound, one kind of pure substance
wrong: A mixture, because anything that can be split up must be a mixture
Mixtures split by physical means; this needed chemical means.
Pure substance.exp: A pure substance is either an element or a compound; one that splits chemically is a compound.

Mixture.q: Two cups of coffee from the same pot taste different: one has more sugar. What does this show?
wrong: Coffee is a compound, since every cup is made from the same coffee beans
It has many substances in it.

Mixture.q: How can you tell a mixture from a compound when separating it?
Mixture.right: A mixture separates by physical means
wrong: A mixture needs electricity or another chemical method to be broken into its parts
Only a compound can be separated
Mixture.exp: Mixtures separate physically; compounds need chemical methods.

Homogeneous mixture.q: Brass looks the same all the way through, but it's made of copper and zinc. What is it?
wrong: A heterogeneous mixture, because it is made of two different metals
You can't see separate parts in brass.
Brass is a mixture of two metals.
Homogeneous mixture.exp: A homogeneous mixture is the same throughout.

Homogeneous mixture.q: Salt is stirred into water until it disappears. What do you have?
wrong: A heterogeneous mixture, because two different substances were put together
Salt and water aren't bonded together.
Homogeneous mixture.exp: Table salt stirred into water is a homogeneous mixture (a solution).

Heterogeneous mixture.q: In oil-and-vinegar dressing you can see two layers. What is it?
wrong: A homogeneous mixture, because it is all poured from a single bottle
Heterogeneous mixture.exp: A heterogeneous mixture has visibly different parts.

wrong: Air, because it is made of many gases mixed together

Solution.q: Which word could replace "homogeneous mixture" in a sentence?
wrong: Suspension, since both words describe something mixed into a liquid
A compound is a pure substance.
Solution.exp: A solution is another name for a homogeneous mixture.

wrong: No, because a solution must always be a liquid like salt water
A solution is any homogeneous mixture.
Your card lists air as homogeneous.
Solution.exp: Air is a homogeneous mixture, so it is a solution.

Subscript.q: How many hydrogen atoms are in one molecule of H₂SO₄?
wrong: 4, because the 4 is the biggest number written in the formula
That's the total of all atoms.
Subscript.exp: A subscript counts the atoms of the element just before it.

Subscript.q: How many atoms in total are in one molecule of CO₂?
wrong: 2, because the 2 at the end of the formula is the total number
There's one C and two O.
Subscript.exp: One carbon plus two oxygen = 3 atoms.

The & symbol.q: A formula code reads "Cu & Zn." What does it describe?
wrong: A compound, because two different elements are written in the same code
The & means the two are just sitting together.
There are two kinds of atoms.
The & symbol.exp: & separates substances that are just sitting together, so it signals a mixture.

The & symbol.q: How do NaCl and "NaCl & H₂O" differ?
The & symbol.right: One is a compound; the other is a mixture
wrong: Both are compounds, because both of them contain sodium chloride
The & makes the second a mixture.
NaCl has two types of atoms.
The & symbol.exp: NaCl alone is a compound; with & H₂O it's a mixture.

wrong: NaHCO₃, because it has more than one kind of atom bonded in it
Several capitals make it a compound.
Element formula clue.exp: One capital letter means one type of atom: an element.

Element formula clue.q: A student says O₃ is a compound because it has a subscript. What's the best reply?
Element formula clue.right: One capital letter means it's an element
wrong: He's right, since any formula with a subscript has to be a compound
A subscript alone doesn't make a compound.
It's a compound because it has 3 atoms
Element formula clue.exp: O₃ has one type of atom, so it is an element; a subscript alone doesn't make a compound.

wrong: Br₂, because it has two atoms bonded together in the same molecule
One type of atom means element.
Compound formula clue.exp: Two or more capital letters bonded with no & means compound.

Compound formula clue.q: NaHCO₃ has how many types of atoms, and what is it?
wrong: 1 type; an element, because it is written as a single formula
Na, H, C and O are four types.
Compound formula clue.exp: Na, H, C and O are bonded in one formula with no &: a compound.

Mixture formula clue.q: Which formula code is a mixture?
wrong: C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁, because it has so many different atoms in a single formula
Mixture formula clue.exp: The & between substances signals a mixture.

Mixture formula clue.q: What should you look for first to sort a formula code into element, compound or mixture?
wrong: The size of the subscripts, since large numbers usually mean a compound
A subscript alone doesn't decide it.
Mixture formula clue.exp: Look for & first: it means mixture. Then count capital letters.

Atom.q: A drawing shows a single unbonded circle labeled Ne. What is it?
wrong: A molecule, because every particle in a drawing counts as a molecule
A molecule is two or more bonded atoms.
A compound has two or more types of atoms.
Atom.exp: An atom is a single particle of an element.

Atom.q: Two oxygen atoms bond together. What do they form?
wrong: A compound, because two atoms are now bonded together into one particle
Both atoms are oxygen, so it's an element.
Atom.exp: Atoms can be bonded together into molecules; O₂ is a molecule of an element.

Molecule.q: Which is a molecule but NOT a compound?
wrong: H₂O, because it has fewer atoms than most of the compounds on your card
H₂O has two types of atoms: a compound.
A single atom isn't a molecule.
Molecule.exp: Br₂ is two bonded atoms of one element: a molecule, but an element.

Molecule.q: What do all molecules have in common?
Molecule.right: Two or more atoms bonded together
wrong: Two or more different types of atoms, like hydrogen and oxygen in water
Br₂ is a molecule with one type.
A molecule has two or more.
Molecule.exp: A molecule is two or more atoms held together by bonds, of one type or several.

Particle.q: A drawing shows 3 single He atoms and 2 O₂ molecules. How many particles are there?
wrong: 7, because each O₂ is two atoms and every atom counts as its own particle
Each molecule counts as one particle.
Particle.exp: Each separate atom or molecule is one particle: 3 + 2 = 5.

Particle.q: Is a single H₂O molecule in a drawing a particle?
Particle.right: Yes; any separate atom or molecule is
wrong: No, because only single atoms count as particles in a drawing
Only if it is a gas
Particle.exp: A particle is any individual atom or molecule.

Bulk terms versus particle terms.q: Which word describes a whole sample, not a single particle?
wrong: Molecule, since a molecule is made of many atoms put together
Bulk terms versus particle terms.exp: Element, compound and mixture describe bulk samples; atom and molecule describe particles.

Bulk terms versus particle terms.q: A jar of pure nitrogen gas (N₂) is described as "a compound because it has molecules." What's wrong?
wrong: Nothing, because any substance made of molecules is a compound
N₂ is a molecule of an element.
Bulk terms versus particle terms.exp: Molecule does NOT equal compound: N₂ molecules have one type of atom, so the sample is an element.

Solvent.q: In salt water, which part is the solvent?
wrong: The salt, because it is the part that dissolves and spreads out

Solvent.q: Sugar dissolves in tea. What is doing the dissolving?
wrong: The sugar, because sugar crystals break down the tea leaves as they dissolve
The cup isn't part of the solution.
Stirring helps, but water is the solvent.
Solvent.exp: Water is the solvent: it does the dissolving.

Solute.q: In lemonade, which ingredient is a solute?
wrong: Water, because it is the part that you can see and pour out of the glass
The glass isn't part of the solution.
Solute.exp: The solute is the part that is dissolved.

Solute.q: Which is the solute in salt water?
wrong: Water, since it is the larger part of the mixture in the glass
Solute.exp: The solute is the dissolved part; the solvent is the part that dissolves it.

Suspension.q: Muddy water is left to stand and the dirt sinks to the bottom. What kind of mixture is it?
wrong: A solution, since the dirt was mixed evenly into the water at first
Suspension.exp: A suspension is a heterogeneous mixture that settles on standing.

Suspension.q: How do a suspension and a colloid differ?
Suspension.right: A suspension settles; a colloid doesn't
wrong: A colloid settles to the bottom over time but a suspension stays mixed
Suspension.exp: A suspension settles on standing; colloids are stable.

Homogeneous examples.q: Which item from the review sheet is homogeneous?
wrong: A chocolate chip cookie, because it's all baked together into a single piece

Homogeneous examples.q: 18K gold and steel are on the same list. Why?
wrong: Both are pure elements, since metals are always made of only one type of atom
Homogeneous examples.exp: 18K gold and steel are homogeneous mixtures.

Heterogeneous examples.q: Which pair from the review sheet are both heterogeneous?
wrong: Rain water and lemonade, because both of them have more than one substance
Heterogeneous examples.exp: Pizza and sand in water have visibly different parts.

Heterogeneous examples.q: A coke float has ice cream floating in soda. Why is it heterogeneous?
wrong: It contains sugar, and anything with sugar in it counts as heterogeneous
Heterogeneous examples.exp: Heterogeneous mixtures have visibly distinguishable parts.

Physical means.q: Which of these is NOT a physical means of separating a mixture?
wrong: Filtration through filter paper to catch an undissolved solid
Physical means.exp: Electrolysis breaks bonds, so it's a chemical method.

Physical means.q: After a mixture is separated by physical means, what is true of its parts?
Physical means.right: Each part is the same substance as before
wrong: Each part has turned into a new substance with new properties of its own
Physical means.exp: Physical means separate a mixture without changing the identity of its parts.

Distillation.q: A mixture of two liquids with different boiling points needs to be separated. Which method fits best?
wrong: Filtration, since the filter paper will catch whichever liquid is thicker
Both are liquids; filtration separates solids from liquids.
Liquids aren't picked up by magnets here.
You can't pick out a liquid.
Distillation.exp: Distillation separates substances by boiling point.

Distillation.q: In distillation, after the liquid boils, what happens to the vapor?
wrong: It is burned off so that only the substance with a high boiling point is left
The vapor is collected, not burned.
Distillation.exp: Distillation boils, then condenses the vapor.

Filtration.q: Sand is stirred into water. Which method separates them most simply?
wrong: Distillation, because the water has a much lower boiling point than sand does
That works but filtration is simpler for an undissolved solid.
That's for parts that stick differently.
Filtration.exp: Filtration separates an undissolved solid from a liquid.

Filtration.q: Salt water is poured through filter paper. What comes out the other side?
wrong: Pure water, because the salt is caught by the tiny holes in the paper
The salt is dissolved in the water.
Filtration.exp: Dissolved salt or sugar passes through a filter.

Chromatography.q: A black marker's ink is separated into blue, red and yellow bands on paper. Which method was used?
wrong: Distillation, because the colors boiled away from the paper at different times
Chromatography.exp: Chromatography separates parts by how strongly they stick to a surface.

Chromatography.q: In chromatography, why do the parts end up at different distances?
Chromatography.right: They stick to the surface by different amounts
wrong: They have different boiling points, so some of them evaporate along the way
Chromatography.exp: Each part adheres differently, so the mobile phase carries each a different distance.

Evaporation.q: Salt water is left in an open dish until only salt crystals remain. Which method is this?
wrong: Filtration, because the salt was trapped and the water passed through
In distillation the vapor is collected; here it just leaves.
Evaporation.exp: Evaporation separates by volatility: the volatile water leaves and the salt stays.

Evaporation.q: What property does evaporation use to separate a mixture?
wrong: Magnetism, because some of the particles are pulled away from the others
How strongly parts stick to paper
Evaporation.exp: Evaporation uses volatility: the volatile part leaves as vapor.

Separating mixtures.q: Which pair of products could come out of separating a mixture physically?
wrong: Hydrogen gas and oxygen gas, which come from water when it is separated
Separating mixtures.exp: Mixtures separate physically into pure substances.

Separating mixtures.q: A sample is separated by filtration into two parts. What was the sample?
wrong: A compound, since it came apart into two different substances in the end
Separating mixtures.exp: Filtration is physical, so the sample was a mixture.

Separating compounds.q: Why can't you separate water into hydrogen and oxygen by filtering it?
wrong: Water is a mixture, but the hydrogen and oxygen are too small for filter paper
Water is a compound; its parts are bonded.
Separating compounds.exp: Compounds need chemical methods, such as electrolysis, to break their bonds.

Separating compounds.q: Which method can separate a compound into its elements?
wrong: Distillation, since it uses heat and heat breaks substances apart
Separating compounds.exp: Compounds need chemical methods like electrolysis or decomposition.

Distillation of salt water.q: After salt water is distilled, what is in the collecting flask, and what stays behind?
wrong: Salt collects in the second flask and pure water stays in the first one
The water boils off; the salt stays.
Distillation of salt water.exp: Distillation boils off the water and condenses it; the salt stays in the flask.

Distillation of salt water.q: Distilling salt water gives salt and water. What kind of change is it?
wrong: Chemical, because the salt water is broken down into two separate substances
Separating a mixture isn't a chemical change.
Salt and water were there all along.
Distillation of salt water.exp: Distillation of salt water is a physical method; no chemical change occurs.

Magnetism.q: Iron filings are mixed into sand. What is the quickest way to separate them?
wrong: Distillation, because iron has a much higher boiling point than sand
That's for parts carried by a liquid.
Magnetism.exp: A magnet picks out the magnetic iron filings.

Magnetism.q: Is pulling iron filings out of sand with a magnet a physical or chemical method?
wrong: Chemical, because the magnet changes the iron into a different form
Magnetism.exp: Magnetism separates without changing the substances, so it's physical.

Mobile phase.q: In paper chromatography of ink, what is the mobile phase?
Mobile phase.right: The water moving up the paper
wrong: The paper, because the colors move along it as they separate
The paper stays put: fixed phase.
Mobile phase.exp: The mobile phase (such as water) carries the mixture's parts across the paper.

Mobile phase.q: What would happen in chromatography with no mobile phase?
wrong: The parts would separate even faster because there is nothing to slow them
The mobile phase is what carries them.
Mobile phase.exp: The mobile phase moves the parts; without it they stay put.

Fixed phase.q: In paper chromatography, which part stays still?
wrong: The water, because it soaks in and stays in the bottom of the beaker
Fixed phase.exp: The fixed phase (such as paper) doesn't move.

Fixed phase.q: A color that sticks strongly to the paper ends up where?
wrong: Farthest from where it started, since it is held tightly by the moving water
Strong sticking to the paper holds it back.
In the water at the bottom
Fixed phase.exp: Parts that stick more to the fixed phase travel less far.

Picking pieces out.q: Which mixture could you separate just by picking pieces out by hand?
wrong: Salt water, since salt crystals are big enough to see and pick out
Dissolved salt can't be picked out.
Picking pieces out.exp: The simplest physical means is picking out pieces by hand, as with a salad.

Picking pieces out.q: Why can you pick the parts out of a jar of jelly beans but not out of salt water?
wrong: Salt water is a compound, so its parts are bonded and can't be picked
Salt water is a mixture, but a homogeneous one.
Picking pieces out.exp: You can pick out visibly separate pieces; a homogeneous mixture has none.

Station 1: paper.q: At Station 1 you tear paper and then ignite it. Which step makes new substances?
wrong: Tearing it, because the paper ends up in smaller and different pieces
Station 1: paper.exp: Tearing is physical; igniting is chemical (flame, heat, ash and gases).

Station 1: paper.q: Which observation from burning the paper shows a chemical change?
wrong: The paper gets smaller as it tears into pieces before it is lit
That's a property, not a change.
That's a property, not a change.
Station 1: paper.exp: Flame, heat, ash and gases are signs of a chemical change.

Station 2: tea lights.q: A tea light melts on a hot plate, then another is lit and burns. How do the changes compare?
Station 2: tea lights.right: Melting is physical; burning is chemical
wrong: Both are chemical, because heat is used to change the wax in each case
Melting doesn't make a new substance.
Melting is chemical; burning is physical
Station 2: tea lights.exp: Melting changes state; burning reacts the wax with oxygen.

Station 2: tea lights.q: When a tea light burns, what does the wax react with?
wrong: The hot plate, since it gives off heat that changes the wax into a new substance
Station 2: tea lights.exp: Burning wax reacts with oxygen and gives off heat and light.

Station 3: steel wool.q: Steel wool is weighed, burned and weighed again. What happens to its mass?
wrong: It decreases, because burning always turns some of the material into smoke
Station 3: steel wool.exp: Iron combines with oxygen to form iron(III) oxide, so the mass goes up.

Station 3: steel wool.q: Burning wood loses mass but burning steel wool gains mass. Why?
Station 3: steel wool.right: The iron combines with oxygen and keeps it
wrong: Steel wool doesn't actually burn; it only melts and absorbs some heat
Station 3: steel wool.exp: The iron combines with oxygen to form iron(III) oxide, so the solid gains mass.

Station 4: vinegar and chalk (TUMS).q: At Station 4, chalk fizzes in vinegar, and then the leftover solid is filtered. Which step is chemical?
wrong: The filtering, because the solid is separated from the leftover liquid
The bubbles show a new gas.
Station 4: vinegar and chalk (TUMS).exp: The bubbles show a chemical change; filtering is a physical separation.

Station 4: vinegar and chalk (TUMS).q: What compound in the chalk (TUMS) reacts with vinegar?
wrong: Sodium chloride, the same compound that is found in ordinary table salt
Station 4: vinegar and chalk (TUMS).exp: Calcium carbonate reacts with vinegar, forming bubbles of gas.

Station 5: zinc in hydrochloric acid.q: A cut post-1982 penny is placed in hydrochloric acid. Why do bubbles form?
Station 5: zinc in hydrochloric acid.right: The zinc core reacts with the acid
wrong: The copper coating boils away because the acid is so much hotter than the penny
Air leaks out of the penny
Station 5: zinc in hydrochloric acid.exp: The zinc core reacts with hydrochloric acid, a chemical change.

Station 5: zinc in hydrochloric acid.q: Why must the penny be cut before it reacts?
wrong: To let the copper coating melt into the acid so that it can react faster
The zinc core is what reacts.
Cutting is to reach the zinc.
Station 5: zinc in hydrochloric acid.exp: A post-1982 penny has a zinc core; once cut, the zinc reacts and the penny loses mass.

Station 6: nail and peroxide.q: At Station 6, hydrogen peroxide is put on an iron nail. What kind of change is this?
wrong: Physical, because the nail keeps its same size and shape the whole time
The peroxide reacts with the iron.
Station 6: nail and peroxide.exp: Hydrogen peroxide reacts with the iron nail, a chemical change.

Station 6: nail and peroxide.q: Why do the safety rules matter at Station 6?
Station 6: nail and peroxide.right: Hydrogen peroxide is a dangerous material
wrong: The iron nail is magnetic and can pull other metal objects off the table
Station 6: nail and peroxide.exp: Hydrogen peroxide is a dangerous material, so the safety rules apply.

Colloid.q: Milk looks smooth and uniform, but it's classified as heterogeneous. How can that be?
wrong: It's a solution, and solutions can be either homogeneous or heterogeneous
Colloid.exp: A colloid is a heterogeneous mixture that may look homogeneous.

wrong: Has visible layers that separate from each other when it is left to stand
Colloid.exp: A colloid may appear homogeneous to the naked eye.

Colloid particle size.q: A mixture's particles are about 500 nm across. Which kind of mixture is it most likely?
wrong: A suspension, because any particles bigger than 100 nm must settle out
Colloid particles run up to 1000 nm.
Colloid particle size.exp: Colloid particles are about 1 to 1000 nm across.

Colloid particle size.q: Which size range belongs to colloid particles?
wrong: Larger than 1 cm, big enough to see with the naked eye and pick out
Colloid particle size.exp: Colloid particles are about 1 nm to 1000 nm across.

Colloid stability.q: A jar of milk and a jar of muddy water sit for a day. What do you expect?
wrong: Both settle into layers, because all heterogeneous mixtures settle over time
Colloid stability.exp: Colloids are stable and don't settle; suspensions do.

Colloid stability.q: Why can't you separate a colloid with filter paper?
Colloid stability.right: Its particles pass through simple filters
wrong: Its particles are so large that they block the filter paper completely
Colloid particles are too small to catch.
Colloid stability.exp: Colloids can't be separated by simple filtration.

Tyndall effect.q: A laser beam shines through two glasses. You can see the beam in one but not the other. Which one is the colloid?
Tyndall effect.right: The one where the beam is visible
wrong: The one where the beam is invisible, because colloids let all light pass straight through
A solution doesn't scatter the beam.
Tyndall effect.exp: Colloid particles scatter light so the beam is visible (Tyndall effect).

Tyndall effect.q: How could you tell salt water (a solution) from a colloid that looks just like it?
Tyndall effect.right: Shine a light beam through each
wrong: Pour each one through filter paper and see which one leaves something behind
Let them sit to see which settles
Tyndall effect.exp: Only the colloid scatters a beam of light (the Tyndall effect).

Brownian movement.q: Under a microscope, tiny particles in a colloid jiggle in random zigzag paths. What is this called?
wrong: The Tyndall effect, because the particles move so fast that they scatter light
Brownian movement.exp: Brownian movement is the continuous, random zigzag motion of colloid particles.

Brownian movement.q: Which describes the path of a colloid particle?
wrong: A straight line down to the bottom of the container, where it settles
Brownian movement.exp: Colloid particles move in a continuous, random zigzag path.

Centrifuge.q: Cream needs to be separated from milk. Filtration doesn't work. What does?
wrong: Distillation, because cream has a much higher boiling point than the rest of the milk
Centrifuge.exp: A high-speed centrifuge can separate a colloid, like cream from milk.

Centrifuge.q: Why is a centrifuge needed for a colloid but not for sand in water?
Centrifuge.right: Colloid particles are too small to filter
wrong: Sand dissolves in the water, so it can't be caught by a centrifuge at all
Sand doesn't dissolve; filtration catches it.
Sand in water is a suspension.
Centrifuge.exp: Colloid particles pass through simple filters, so the colloid has to be spun.

Dispersed phase.q: In fog, tiny water droplets are spread through air. Which is the dispersed phase?
wrong: The air, because it surrounds the droplets and is spread all through the fog
Air is the larger amount: the dispersion medium.
Dispersed phase.exp: The dispersed phase is the smaller amount spread through the mixture.

Dispersed phase.q: The dispersed phase in a colloid is most like which part of a solution?
wrong: The solvent, because it's the part that the other particles are spread through
Dispersed phase.exp: The dispersed phase is the smaller amount, like a solute.

Dispersion medium.q: In whipped cream, gas bubbles are spread through a liquid. What is the dispersion medium?
wrong: The gas bubbles, because they take up most of the space you see
The bubbles are the dispersed phase.
Dispersion medium.exp: The dispersion medium is the larger amount that the particles are spread through.

Dispersion medium.q: The dispersion medium of a colloid is most like which part of a solution?
wrong: The solute, because it is the part of the colloid that gets spread around
Dispersion medium.exp: The dispersion medium is the larger amount, like a solvent.

Aerosol.q: Smoke is solid particles in air, and fog is liquid droplets in air. What type of colloid are both?
wrong: Foams, because both of them have a gas as one of their two parts
A foam is gas in a liquid.
Gel is liquid in a solid.
Aerosol.exp: An aerosol is a solid or liquid dispersed in a gas.

Aerosol.q: Insecticide spray and dust are both aerosols. What do they have in common?
Aerosol.right: Both are dispersed in a gas
wrong: Both are liquid droplets spread through a solid such as a wall or carpet
Aerosols are dispersed in a gas.
Spray is liquid; dust is solid.
Aerosol.exp: An aerosol is any solid or liquid dispersed in a gas.

Foam.q: Soap lather is gas trapped in a liquid. What type of colloid is it?
wrong: Aerosol, because it has gas in it, like the air in the bubbles
An aerosol is dispersed IN a gas.
Foam.exp: A foam is a gas dispersed in a liquid.

Foam.q: How is a foam the reverse of a liquid aerosol like fog?
Foam.right: Foam is gas in liquid; fog is liquid in gas
wrong: Foam is solid in gas and fog is gas in solid, so they swap their states
Check the states: foam is gas in a liquid.
Foam.exp: Foam: gas dispersed in a liquid. Fog: liquid dispersed in a gas.

Emulsion.q: Milk is droplets of fat (a liquid) spread through water. What type of colloid is it?
wrong: Foam, because it is white and can be whipped into a fluffy mixture
Foam is gas in a liquid.
Emulsion.exp: An emulsion is a liquid dispersed in a liquid.

Emulsion.q: Which pair are both emulsions on your card?
wrong: Whipped cream and soap lather, because both of them are white and fluffy
Emulsion.exp: Milk, hair cream and butter are emulsions.

Sol.q: Paint is solid pigment particles spread through a liquid. What type of colloid is it?
wrong: Gel, because the paint becomes solid as it dries on the wall
Gel is liquid in a solid.
Sol.exp: A sol is a solid dispersed in a liquid.

Sol.q: How does a sol differ from a gel?
Sol.right: Sol: solid in liquid. Gel: liquid in solid
wrong: Sol: liquid in solid, and gel: solid in liquid, the reverse of what most think
Both are gas in a solid
Sol.exp: A sol is solid in liquid; a gel is liquid in solid.

Gel.q: Jelly is liquid held inside a solid network. What type of colloid is it?
wrong: Sol, because it contains a solid and a liquid mixed together evenly
Sol is solid in a liquid; jelly is liquid in a solid.
Gel.exp: A gel is a liquid dispersed in a solid.

Gel.q: Which example from your cards is a gel?
wrong: Butter, because it is soft and contains water mixed into a solid
Your card lists butter as an emulsion.

Solid sol.q: Pumice stone is gas bubbles trapped in a solid. What type of colloid is it?
wrong: Foam, because foams are always made of gas bubbles trapped in something
Foam is gas in a liquid.
Solid sol.exp: A solid sol is a solid or gas dispersed in a solid; pumice is gas in a solid.

Solid sol.q: Colored glass and foam rubber are both solid sols. What do they share?
Solid sol.right: Both are dispersed in a solid
wrong: Both have liquid droplets spread through a gas, like a mist that hardened
Solid sol.exp: Solid sols have a solid or gas dispersed in a solid.
